title: Vidar Infostealer Uses Custom Virtual Machine and Stream Ciphers to Evade Malware Analysis
content_md: Vidar, a well-known information-stealing malware family first seen in 2018, has introduced new string-obfuscation methods designed to slow down security researchers and automated malware-analysis systems. Researchers at Zscaler ThreatLabz tracked Vidar samples between May and early September 2026 and found that the malware moved from basic XOR string encryption to modified ChaCha20 routines, and later to a custom virtual machine combined with a changing stream cipher. The updates make each Vidar build look different at the code level, even when it performs the same functions. This approach can reduce the effectiveness of static signatures, which often rely on predictable strings, constants, or byte patterns to identify malware. Vidar is commonly used to collect browser data, cryptocurrency wallet information, stored credentials, plugins, and other victim-system data. The malware’s latest protection layers aim to hide operational strings such as error messages, browser collection details, and HTTP headers until runtime. Vidar VM Cipher Evasion In Vidar versions 2.x and 3.x, the malware uses a lightweight custom virtual machine to decode protected strings. The VM runs a bytecode interpreter that follows a fetch-decode-execute process. Each byte in the embedded bytecode acts as an opcode.
